paragraphs: Training a regression model can involve buying data from people who choose how much effort to invest. The learner wants accurate contributions but cannot directly verify their quality. This paper studies repeated data acquisition, where the prospect of receiving future work can encourage workers to provide better data today.

The proposed SR-UCB framework combines a bandit-style selection index with a simple payment rule. Each worker’s index approximates the quality of previous contributions and helps determine future assignments. The mechanism therefore connects present effort to future opportunities. Its indexes can be updated online, keeping the ongoing computation light.

For linear regression and a specified family of nonlinear regression problems, the authors establish an approximate Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which workers exert the learner’s chosen target effort. The approximation improves as the number of acquisition stages grows. A private variant also provides differential privacy for workers’ data, with a weaker incentive guarantee. These results make repeated participation central to both the acquisition strategy and its incentive analysis.
neurips-2016-a-bandit-framework-for-stra.tldr: SR-UCB uses future work opportunities to encourage high-quality regression data, with approximate equilibrium guarantees and a private variant.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning analyses depend on Bregman divergences, a family of measures for comparing points. This paper expands where those analytical tools can be used. Its theorem shows that certain Bregman distortions, including ones generated by potentially nonconvex functions, can be rewritten exactly as scaled Bregman divergences after transforming the data.

The transformation provides two ways to understand the result. Geometrically, it preserves the relevant comparison up to scaling while allowing adaptive metrics. From an optimization perspective, it connects generalized perspective transforms. Admissible distortions include geodesic distances on curved manifolds and distortions involving projections or gauge normalization. The exact rewriting lets existing Bregman theory support analysis in these settings.

The authors develop three applications: reducing multiclass density-ratio estimation to class-probability estimation, constructing an adaptive mirror-descent algorithm that enforces a norm without projections, and reducing clustering on flat manifolds to clustering on curved manifolds. Experiments in all three domains support the analyses. Together, these applications illustrate the theorem’s usefulness across estimation, optimization, and clustering.
neurips-2016-a-scaled-bregman-theorem-wi.tldr: A new theorem rewrites certain geometric distortions as scaled Bregman divergences, extending familiar analytical tools to several learning problems.

paragraphs: A classification ensemble combines predictions from multiple classifiers through voting. Computing every vote can be unnecessary when the eventual result is already sufficiently clear. This paper studies how to estimate confidence in the final vote while observing only part of a parallel randomized ensemble.

For a particular test example, the authors represent classifiers as marbles in an urn, with each marble’s color indicating its predicted class. Querying successive classifiers corresponds to drawing marbles without replacement. Analysis using the hypergeometric distribution estimates confidence in the full ensemble’s decision from the votes observed so far. Prediction can stop once that confidence reaches a sufficiently high level.

The framework also accommodates prior knowledge about possible voting outcomes. With a uniform prior, its analysis is equivalent to an earlier approach using Dirichlet distributions. Its advantage is the ease of incorporating problem-specific knowledge through Bayesian reasoning. The authors show that this knowledge can accelerate classification and support advance estimates of the expected average speed-up.
neurips-2016-an-urn-model-for-majority-v.tldr: An urn-based analysis lets ensembles stop querying classifiers once confidence in the final vote is sufficiently high.

paragraphs: Topic models aim to recover themes from collections of documents. Many identification guarantees assume anchor words: words that occur with positive probability in only one topic. Alternatives have relaxed this assumption using higher-order corpus statistics, but those statistics are difficult to estimate reliably, and the associated models depend on topics being uncorrelated.

This paper develops an anchor-free framework using second-order moments. It guarantees topic identification under a condition described as substantially milder than the anchor-word assumption. The framework addresses correlated topic modeling while reducing reliance on difficult higher-order estimates. Identification matters because it concerns whether the underlying topics can be distinguished from the information the model uses.

The associated algorithm requires one eigen-decomposition and a few small linear programs, supporting straightforward implementation and scaling to large problems. Experiments on TDT2 and Reuters-21578 show favorable results relative to prior approaches on coherence, similarity count, and clustering accuracy. The theoretical guarantee and empirical findings together support the practicality of relaxing the anchor-word requirement.
neurips-2016-anchor-free-correlated-topi.tldr: An anchor-free topic model uses second-order statistics to identify topics under a milder condition and performs favorably on two corpora.

paragraphs: The restricted isometry property, or RIP, gives guarantees for recovering sparse signals from linear measurements. It is especially valuable for computationally efficient recovery methods. Checking RIP is generally NP-hard, motivating attempts to develop tractable certificates that can establish when a matrix has the property.

This paper examines average-case certifiers. Such a certifier must never incorrectly declare that a matrix satisfies RIP, while succeeding often on random instances. This separates the demand for trustworthy positive answers from the demand to handle every possible input. Tractable certifiers already exist in a parameter regime that the abstract describes as suboptimal.

The authors show that improving on that regime is computationally hard under a new, weaker assumption concerning dense-subgraph detection. The conclusion is conditional on this hardness assumption. Its significance is that random inputs do not automatically make reliable RIP certification easy: requiring certificates to avoid false positive declarations can preserve a computational barrier even in an average-case setting.
neurips-2016-average-case-hardness-of-ri.tldr: Under a dense-subgraph detection assumption, reliable average-case RIP certification is computationally hard beyond a known suboptimal regime.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a way to train neural networks whose weights and activations are binary at run time. Binary weights and activations are also used when computing training gradients. The approach makes a highly restricted numerical representation part of the network’s training procedure and eventual execution.

During the forward pass, binary representations sharply reduce memory requirements and memory accesses. They also allow most arithmetic operations to be replaced by bitwise operations. The authors expect these changes to substantially improve power efficiency. This expectation follows the computational design; the abstract’s reported runtime result concerns a specific binary matrix-multiplication implementation.

Experiments using Torch7 and Theano achieve nearly state-of-the-art results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN, with preliminary findings also reported for ImageNet. A binary GPU kernel runs the MNIST network seven times faster than an unoptimized GPU kernel without losing classification accuracy. That comparison demonstrates a concrete implementation benefit alongside the broader evidence that binary networks can retain strong predictive performance.
neurips-2016-binarized-neural-networks-b.tldr: Binary weights and activations enable compact neural networks with strong benchmark accuracy and a demonstrated GPU speed-up over an unoptimized kernel.

paragraphs: When a dataset has far more features than observations, splitting work by features can reduce problem size more effectively than splitting by examples. Existing feature-partitioning approaches, however, can struggle with strong correlations or fail to reduce the model dimension sufficiently. DECO addresses these obstacles in distributed variable selection and parameter estimation.

The framework partitions variables among multiple workers and fits decorrelated subset data at each worker. Each worker can use an algorithm designed for high-dimensional problems. The decorrelation step is central: it supports local estimation after the original feature space has been divided into smaller pieces that can be processed in parallel.

The authors establish consistent variable selection and parameter estimation on each subset with almost no assumptions, retaining that qualification. They also obtain convergence rates that are nearly minimax optimal for sparse and weakly sparse models and do not depend on the number of partitions. Numerical experiments illustrate the framework’s performance. The theoretical results connect computational partitioning with statistical accuracy across the distributed subsets.
neurips-2016-decorrelated-feature-space-.tldr: DECO decorrelates partitioned features to support parallel sparse regression with nearly minimax convergence rates independent of the partition count.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains hidden layers by passing an output error backward through successive layers. Feedback alignment had shown that backward connections can use random weights instead of matching forward weights. This paper extends that principle by sending the output error directly to each hidden layer through fixed random connections.

These direct connections let hidden layers learn more independently of the rest of the network, including from a zero initial condition. The method can reach zero training error in convolutional and very deep networks without backpropagating error layer by layer. The authors also present it as a step toward biological plausibility because its error signal is almost local and it needs no symmetric or reciprocal weights.

For fully connected networks, experiments on MNIST and CIFAR yield test performance almost as good as backpropagation. With dropout, the method reaches 1.45% error on permutation-invariant MNIST. These findings distinguish the ability to fit training data from the reported generalization results, while showing that direct random feedback can provide useful learning signals.
neurips-2016-direct-feedback-alignment-p.tldr: Fixed random connections can send output error directly to hidden layers and train deep networks without layer-by-layer error backpropagation.

paragraphs: Feature selection needs to recognize when several features provide useful information jointly. Methods that score features without adequately representing these interactions can overlook high-order dependencies. This paper introduces CMICOT, a filter method that extends sequential forward selection using scores based on conditional mutual information.

The authors formulate a new max-min, or saddle-point, optimization problem to construct the scoring function. Its purpose is to identify interactions among several features as the selected set grows. Directly estimating mutual information in this high-dimensional setting requires prohibitively many samples. CMICOT reduces that burden through a greedy approximation and binary representatives, making the proposed interaction-sensitive score usable in practice.

Experiments compare the method with recently proposed interaction-aware filters and several leading filters that do not account for interactions, using ten public benchmark datasets. The authors report superior performance in these comparisons. The contribution combines a scoring formulation for high-order dependence with an approximation strategy that addresses the statistical cost of estimating it.
neurips-2016-efficient-high-order-intera.tldr: CMICOT selects features using an interaction-sensitive information score made practical through greedy approximation and binary representatives.

paragraphs: A generative neural sampler turns a random input vector into a sample from a distribution determined by its weights. Such networks can generate samples and compute derivatives efficiently, but the models considered here do not support likelihood computation or marginalization. Adversarial training addresses training through an auxiliary discriminative neural network.

This paper places that training method within a broader mathematical framework. The authors show that generative-adversarial training is a special case of an existing approach to variational divergence estimation. A divergence measures disagreement between distributions, so the connection gives a general way to express the training objective in terms of the difference between generated and target distributions.

The central result is that any f-divergence can be used to train these generative networks. This opens a family of training objectives within the same overarching framework. The paper discusses how different divergence choices affect training complexity and the quality of the resulting models. Its contribution is this generalization and analysis of choices, without asserting that one divergence is universally best.
neurips-2016-f-gan-training-generative-n.tldr: f-GAN generalizes adversarial training by showing that any f-divergence can serve as an objective for training generative neural samplers.

paragraphs: The initial centers chosen for k-means strongly influence the quality of the resulting clustering. The widely used k-means++ seeding procedure becomes costly on massive datasets because it is inherently sequential and requires a full pass through the data for each of the k centers. This makes initialization itself a scaling obstacle.

Earlier work used Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to approximate k-means++ seeding efficiently, but its guarantees depended on assumptions about the data-generating distribution. This paper proposes a simple, fast seeding algorithm with provable clustering quality that does not require assumptions on the data. Removing those distributional requirements broadens the scope of the guarantee.

The analysis establishes a favorable trade-off between solution quality and computational cost, with seeding speed-ups of up to several orders of magnitude over k-means++. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the theoretical results. The contribution therefore concerns both how quickly initial centers can be obtained and what quality guarantees remain available when reducing that computational expense.
neurips-2016-fast-and-provably-good-seed.tldr: A fast k-means seeding algorithm offers provable clustering quality without assumptions on the data and a favorable quality–cost trade-off.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a policy from examples of expert behavior when the learner cannot interact with the expert and has no reinforcement signal. A conventional route first infers the expert’s cost function through inverse reinforcement learning, then runs reinforcement learning to obtain a policy. That two-stage process can be slow and indirect.

The authors propose a general framework that extracts a policy directly from demonstration data, with the intended effect of applying reinforcement learning after inverse reinforcement learning. This connection matters because it links direct imitation to the optimization perspective of the two-stage approach, while avoiding the need to treat recovering a cost function as a separate intermediate objective.

A particular instance of the framework connects imitation learning with generative adversarial networks. From that connection, the authors derive a model-free imitation algorithm. They report significant performance gains over existing model-free methods when imitating complex behavior in large, high-dimensional environments. The findings support the effectiveness of this adversarial formulation for the evaluated imitation problems.
neurips-2016-generative-adversarial-imit.tldr: An adversarial imitation framework learns policies directly from expert demonstrations and improves performance on complex, high-dimensional imitation tasks.

paragraphs: A structured superposition model describes observations using parameters that are sums of differently structured components. One example is a matrix expressed as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix. The statistical task includes estimating the individual pieces, making their separate recoverability an important part of the problem.

This paper treats a general setting with any number of components, each described through a norm. The authors provide a simple estimator and a geometric condition under which the components can be estimated accurately. That condition ties the possibility of separating the components to the geometry of their structures, rather than restricting the analysis to a single predefined combination.

The analysis characterizes sample complexity and provides finite-sample bounds on the estimation error of each component. It uses empirical-process tools and generic chaining, with results expressed through Gaussian widths of suitable spherical caps. These geometric quantities organize the statistical guarantees. The resulting framework substantially generalizes earlier work on superposition models while retaining component-specific accuracy statements.
neurips-2016-high-dimensional-structured.tldr: A general estimator separates sums of norm-structured components under a geometric condition, with sample-complexity and componentwise error guarantees.

paragraphs: Recognizing facial action units from spontaneous expressions is difficult when only limited labeled training images are available. Convolutional networks can overfit those images and generalize poorly to unseen people. This paper introduces Incremental Boosting CNN, or IB-CNN, to address that problem by integrating boosting into the network.

Its incremental boosting layer selects discriminative neurons from the layer below and updates across successive mini-batches. The authors also introduce a loss function that accounts for errors made by both the combined boosted classifier and its individual weak classifiers. Fine-tuning therefore considers the quality of the component classifiers alongside the performance of their combination.

Across four benchmark action-unit databases, IB-CNN significantly improves on a traditional CNN and a boosting CNN without incremental learning. It also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art CNN methods. The gains are especially pronounced for action units with the lowest frequencies in the databases. These findings support the usefulness of incremental boosting when labeled examples are limited and some target units appear infrequently.
neurips-2016-incremental-boosting-convol.tldr: IB-CNN integrates incremental boosting into a convolutional network and improves facial action-unit recognition, especially for infrequent units.

paragraphs: Price optimization uses demand forecasts to choose prices that maximize revenue or profit. Forecasting methods can describe price–demand relationships across many products, but turning those forecasts into optimal prices can be computationally expensive. The paper identifies this optimization cost as a barrier for existing methods, including mixed-integer programming formulations.

The proposed approach connects a mathematical property of revenue, supermodularity, with cross elasticity of demand: how demand for one product responds to another product’s price. This connection enables an algorithm based on network flow. Under an assumption about cross elasticity, the algorithm returns an exact optimal solution and can handle hundreds or thousands of products.

The authors also examine cases where that assumption does not hold. In those experiments, the method efficiently finds approximate solutions whose quality matches other state-of-the-art approaches. The distinction matters: exact optimality is conditional, while performance outside the condition is supported empirically. The contribution combines a scalable computational approach with a clear structural basis for its strongest guarantee.
neurips-2016-large-scale-price-optimizat.tldr: A network-flow approach scales price optimization to many products, with exact solutions under a cross-elasticity assumption and competitive approximations empirically.

paragraphs: A rational decision can be modeled as the solution to an optimization problem, but an observer may know only part of that problem. This paper studies predicting the solution of a linear program when some objectives or constraints are unknown. It generalizes learning from revealed preferences, where observed choices provide information about an agent’s unknown goals.

In the first setting, the learner knows the objective but does not know an arbitrary, fixed collection of constraints. Each example adds a known constraint, and the learner predicts the optimum under both the hidden and visible constraints. This represents an agent whose goals are understood but whose available resources are hidden.

In the second setting, the objective is unknown and changes in a controlled way. Constraints can also change each day, but they are known, and each example supplies partial information about the objective. The authors give mistake-bound learning algorithms for both settings. These results frame prediction under incomplete optimization knowledge as a learning problem with guarantees on accumulated prediction errors.
neurips-2016-learning-from-rational-beha.tldr: Mistake-bound algorithms predict linear-program solutions when constraints are hidden or an unknown objective changes in a controlled way.

paragraphs: Facility-location objectives are used to select summaries of large datasets, with additional uses in sensor placement, retrieval, and clustering. A computational obstacle is evaluating pairwise benefits across all items. For large collections, this can be infeasible, motivating approaches that calculate benefits only between nearby items.

Previous guarantees for this nearest-neighbor sparsification required several strong additional assumptions. The authors show that those extra assumptions are unnecessary: solving the sparsified problem can be almost optimal under the problem’s standard assumptions. The result gives stronger theoretical support for reducing the number of pairwise relationships represented in the optimization.

The paper also analyzes another form of sparsification that better captures methods such as Locality Sensitive Hashing, which can accelerate nearest-neighbor computations. This analysis extends the approach to a broader family of similarities. Demonstrations show rapid generation of interpretable summaries. Together, the results address both the quality retained after sparsification and the practical work needed to obtain the sparse relationships.
neurips-2016-leveraging-sparsity-for-eff.tldr: Sparse facility-location problems can yield almost-optimal summaries under standard assumptions, with further analysis supporting faster neighbor computations.

paragraphs: Selecting a diverse subset arises in recommendation, search, feature selection, and data summarization. The items can be represented as points in a metric space, with distances supporting a chosen notion of diversity. Selection must also respect restrictions such as a fixed subset size or a more general matroid constraint.

This paper develops a linear-programming framework for constructing approximation algorithms for these problems. For the objective called sum-min diversity, the authors obtain the first constant-factor approximation algorithm. The framework can also incorporate additional constraints and secondary objectives, making it useful when diversity is one part of a more constrained selection task.

The paper complements this algorithmic result with hardness results for two natural diversity objectives, conditional on the planted-clique assumption. Empirical evaluation examines approximation quality against the linear-programming objective and compares selected subsets with those produced by other popular diversity algorithms. These experiments assess the framework from two perspectives: its relation to the relaxation and the practical quality of its selections.
neurips-2016-linear-relaxations-for-find.tldr: A linear-programming framework yields a constant-factor approximation for sum-min diversity while accommodating extra constraints and secondary objectives.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary matrix completion as an online prediction problem. On each trial, the learner predicts a matrix entry and then sees its true value. The goal is to control the number of incorrect predictions accumulated as information about the matrix arrives over time.

The authors propose a Matrix Exponentiated Gradient algorithm and prove a mistake bound that scales with the matrix’s margin complexity. The bound supports an interpretation in which each row is a prediction task and the columns are the objects being predicted. This makes the matrix-completion problem a collection of related prediction tasks within one analytical framework.

Using that interpretation, the authors show that the algorithm’s mistake count is comparable, up to a logarithmic factor, to a Kernel Perceptron using an optimal kernel chosen in hindsight. They also discuss predicting as well as the best biclustering and predicting graph labels without knowing the graph beforehand. These applications illustrate how the guarantee can extend beyond filling an isolated table of binary values.
neurips-2016-mistake-bounds-for-binary-m.tldr: An online binary-matrix predictor has a margin-complexity mistake bound comparable to a hindsight-optimal Kernel Perceptron up to a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: Manifold learning often seeks an embedding that preserves the geometry of the data with little distortion. A difficulty is that intrinsic dimension and the dimension needed for an isometric embedding can differ. Data with intrinsic dimension d may require more than d embedding dimensions to preserve its geometry without distortion.

The paper proposes an algorithm that can work with this higher-dimensional possibility, which many geometry-preserving methods cannot accommodate. For any proposed embedding, it directly computes a distortion loss and repeatedly updates the embedded coordinates to reduce that loss. This makes geometric distortion an explicit quantity guiding the optimization.

The loss is based on the push-forward Riemannian metric associated with the embedding coordinates, linking the objective to the geometry induced by those coordinates. Experiments show superior performance in obtaining low-distortion embeddings. The contribution is therefore an approach that measures and reduces distortion directly while allowing the embedding dimension to exceed the data’s intrinsic dimension when preserving geometry calls for it.
neurips-2016-nearly-isometric-embedding-.tldr: An embedding algorithm directly reduces geometric distortion and can use more dimensions than the data’s intrinsic dimension.

paragraphs: The perceptron is a model for learning a separating hyperplane. This paper develops two quantum algorithms for perceptron learning and analyzes improvements in computational and statistical complexity. The algorithms target different quantities: the dependence on the number of training points and the dependence of the mistake bound on the margin.

The first algorithm determines a separating hyperplane in O(sqrt(N)) steps, where N is the number of data points. This is sublinear in dataset size. The second changes the stated classical mistake bound from O(1/gamma²) to O(1/sqrt(gamma)), where gamma denotes the margin. These are distinct guarantees, describing dataset-size scaling and margin-dependent prediction complexity respectively.

Both improvements use quantum amplitude amplification applied to a version-space interpretation of the perceptron. That interpretation organizes learning around candidate separators consistent with the learning problem. The paper’s contribution is to show how this viewpoint supports quantum improvements in the stated complexity measures, giving two algorithmic routes for enhancing perceptron learning through quantum computation.
neurips-2016-quantum-perceptron-models-c.tldr: Two quantum perceptron algorithms improve dataset-size scaling and margin-dependent mistake bounds using amplitude amplification.

paragraphs: Graph partitioning divides a graph into groups, and the objective determines which divisions the algorithm prefers. This paper introduces Product Cut, a multiplicative cut-based objective for dividing a graph into multiple groups. The contribution includes both a way to formulate the partitioning task and an algorithm for optimizing that formulation.

The authors investigate the objective’s mathematical properties in detail, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed model. This analysis matters because introducing a new partitioning score creates two connected questions: what mathematical structure the score has, and how an algorithm can use that structure to search for a partition. The paper addresses the objective and its optimization within one framework.

The corresponding algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark datasets used in the study. That reported finding supports the practical effectiveness of Product Cut alongside its mathematical development. The resulting contribution is a theoretically grounded alternative for multi-way graph partitioning whose proposed optimization algorithm also performs strongly in the reported benchmark comparisons.
neurips-2016-the-product-cut-a7347cdac1.tldr: Product Cut introduces a multiplicative objective for multi-way graph partitioning with mathematical analysis and strong benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks a function’s maximum, while level-set estimation determines which points fall on either side of a threshold. TruVaR handles both tasks within a Gaussian-process framework. The shared idea is to reduce uncertainty over the points that still matter to the task’s unresolved decisions.

At each step, the algorithm greedily reduces a sum of truncated variances. For optimization, the relevant set contains potential maximizers; for level-set estimation, it contains points that remain unclassified. Confidence bounds update these sets as evidence accumulates. This formulation accommodates point-specific evaluation costs and noise that varies across points, features that can be difficult to incorporate into myopic algorithms.

The authors provide a general theoretical guarantee covering these settings and use it to recover and strengthen existing results for both tasks. They also establish a result for choosing among noise levels with associated costs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The framework thus connects uncertainty reduction with practical decisions about where, and at what measurement cost, to gather information.
neurips-2016-truncated-variance-reductio.tldr: TruVaR unifies Bayesian optimization and level-set estimation by reducing relevant uncertainty while accommodating varying measurement costs and noise.

paragraphs: Large convex optimization problems may contain components whose importance differs over the course of solving them. Identifying the important components quickly can help an algorithm converge faster. This paper develops a general approach to doing so by exploiting piecewise linear structure in the optimization problem.

The authors formulate the task as minimizing a sum of piecewise functions. From this formulation, they derive a principled mechanism for using the structure, leading to a theoretically justified working-set algorithm and a new screening test. These results generalize and improve on earlier methods for exploiting structure. The working-set approach concentrates computation on a selected collection of components.

The empirical study focuses on scalability and finds a meaningful difference between the two approaches. Screening scales surprisingly poorly as problem size grows, while the working-set algorithm convincingly outperforms the alternatives tested. The findings show that having a principled screening rule does not by itself ensure favorable scaling, and support the proposed working-set method in the evaluated problems.
neurips-2016-unified-methods-for-exploit.tldr: A unified piecewise formulation yields screening and working-set methods, with the working-set algorithm showing stronger empirical scalability.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis aims to recover underlying sources from nonlinear observations, making it appealing for unsupervised feature learning. A central obstacle is identifiability: the earlier models discussed in the abstract do not determine a unique source explanation. This paper uses changes in a time series’ statistical structure to address that obstacle.

The proposed principle, time-contrastive learning, learns a representation that optimally distinguishes different time windows. Its learning signal comes from temporal nonstationarity. The authors then connect this discrimination task to a nonlinear ICA model redefined to include those temporal changes, giving the learned features a source-recovery interpretation.

When combined with linear ICA, time-contrastive learning estimates that nonlinear ICA model up to pointwise transformations of the sources. The solution is unique within this remaining ambiguity. The authors present this as the first rigorous, constructive, and very general identifiability result for nonlinear ICA. The qualification about source transformations is essential: the guarantee identifies the model to that equivalence, rather than recovering a completely fixed numerical representation of every source.
neurips-2016-unsupervised-feature-extrac.tldr: Time-contrastive learning uses temporal nonstationarity to identify a nonlinear ICA model up to pointwise source transformations.
